```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")

read_json5_clean <- function (path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  jsonlite::fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

summary_cache <- jsonlite::fromJSON("modern_arabian_peninsula_summary_cache.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
region_json <- read_json5_clean("modern_arabian_peninsula.json5")
ledger_json <- read_json5_clean("modern_arabian_peninsula_source_ledger.json5")
sett_json <- jsonlite::fromJSON("modern_arabian_peninsula_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

# Abstract

Between the British military withdrawal from the Persian Gulf in 1971AD and 2026AD, the Arabian Peninsula underwent the swiftest sustained population expansion of any major world region. Across a domain covering 2,78M km² in Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, total population multiplied nearly six-and-a-half times, rising from 14,6M in 1971AD to 22,4M in 1980AD, 37,8M in 1992AD, 55,6M in 2004AD, 76,4M in 2015AD, 88,9M in 2022AD and 94,8M in 2025AD. That 3,53% compound annual growth rate fused two structurally opposite demographic regimes. Along the hydrocarbon-rich Gulf littoral and inside Saudi Arabia's central plateau, state-led oil investment, desalinated water networks and contract labour recruitment under the sponsorship system transformed pearling ports and oasis settlements into metropolitan corridors led at peak by Ar-Riyāḍ (7,68M in 2017AD; 7,46M in 2025AD), Jiddah (4,7M in 2021AD; 4M in 2025AD), Dubayy (3,75M), Al-Kuwayt (2,99M metropolitan peak in 2018AD), Makkah (2,57M), Abū Ẓaby (1,84M), Al-Madīnah (1,52M), Ad-Dammām (1,49M), Muscat (1,42M in 2019AD) and Ad-Dawḥah (1,31M peak; 988,2k in 2025AD). Along the south-western mountain escarpment, by contrast, Yemen combined prolonged high rural fertility, minimal foreign immigration and severe post-2014 conflict displacement centred on Ṣan'ā' (2,58M peak; 2,29M in 2025AD), Aden (1,15M) and Ta'izz (626,6k). HANDBOOK reconciles 5.250 catalogued urban and rural localities with 233 first- and second-order administrative census units across all seven sovereign states using strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic scaling over metric-isotropic radial distance fields and non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging.

# Background

Geography divides the modern Arabian Peninsula into three distinct demographic environments whose ecological limits were overridden—though never erased—after 1971AD by fossil energy and desalination. The largest territory by far is the arid interior shield and sedimentary desert spanning Najd, Al-Hasa, the Northern Borders and the Rub' al-Khali, where mean annual rainfall drops below 100 mm and permanent settlement historically clung to artesian springs, caravan wells and wadi oases [@Arabia2022Saudi]. Once oil revenues funded deep-aquifer pumping, coastal desalination plants and arterial highways during the 1970s and 1980s, Ar-Riyāḍ, Buraydah, Al-Hufūf and the Jubail-Dammam industrial corridor broke free of local oasis ceilings and absorbed millions of internal migrants and foreign workers [@Wagle2024Labor; @Hkiri2025Correlatin]. A second zone comprises the shallow Gulf littoral from Kuwait Bay through Bahrain, Qatar and the Trucial coast to the Batinah plain of Oman, where maritime trading towns turned port infrastructure, free zones and liquefied natural gas exports into hyper-urban city-states with foreign-born resident majorities [@Dito2013Arab; @Valenta2017Comparativ].

The third environment is the rugged south-western highland crescent stretching from 'Asir and Jazan across North Yemen to the Hadhramaut plateau and Dhofar. Here, summer monsoon rains caught at elevations between 1.500 m and 3.000 m sustained terraced sorghum, millet, coffee and qat cultivation alongside dense rural villages centuries before modern petroleum extraction [@Arabia2022Saudi]. Whereas the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) monarchies experienced rapid fertility decline among citizens after the 1990s—offset by vast circular inflows of South Asian, Arab and East African contract workers—Yemen retained high natural increase into the early twenty-first century while exporting remittances-sending labourers northward until the geopolitical rupture of 1990AD [@Dito2013Arab; @Hameed2021India].

Political consolidation after 1971AD established the statistical jurisdictions analysed in this chapter. Following Kuwait's earlier independence (1961) and the withdrawal of British treaty protection from the lower Gulf in 1971AD, Bahrain, Qatar and the seven Trucial Emirates (merged as the United Arab Emirates in December 1971, joined by Ras Al Khaymah in February 1972) assumed direct authority over national civil registration and population counts [@Dito2013Arab; @Emirates2011Employer]. In Oman, the accession of Sultan Qaboos bin Said in July 1970 ended decades of interior isolation and Dhofari insurgency, inaugurating modern provincial administration across Muscat, the Batinah coast and Dhofar [@ALFARHAN2019Migrant]. Yemen remained divided between the Yemen Arab Republic (North Yemen) and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen (South Yemen) until their unification in May 1990, an event followed within three months by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and the mass expulsion of roughly 800k Yemeni workers from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait [@Wagle2024Labor; @Valenta2017Comparativ].

Urbanisation and migration policies since 1992AD further widened the structural gulf between the northern hydrocarbon monarchies and the peninsula's south-western corner. Across Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman, the *kafala* sponsorship regime linked residence visas directly to employment contracts, allowing states to expand or contract urban labour pools rapidly in response to oil price cycles, mega-project construction booms and nationalisation quotas such as Saudisation (*Nitaqat*), Emiratisation and Omanisation [@Valenta2017Comparativ; @Hameed2021India; @Thomas2025Employabil]. Meanwhile, Saudi Vision 2030, Qatar's World Cup infrastructure programme and Emirati logistics and tourism hubs drove unprecedented metropolitan concentration along highway corridors [@Arabia2022Saudi; @Ageeli2019Applicatio]. Across the southern border in Yemen, political upheaval after 2011 and full-scale civil war from March 2015 halted national census-taking altogether, crippled Red Sea ports and displaced millions internally toward highland cities such as Ṣan'ā', Ibb, Dhamār and Ma'rib [@VERWIMP2007Child].

# Methodology

HANDBOOK models the Arabian Peninsula from 1971AD to 2026AD under Regime 3, combining sovereign national census series, subadministrative boundary polygons and urban settlement trajectories onto a continuous 5-arcminute demographic grid. Across the seven states, the spatial mask encompasses 35.297 terrestrial cells organised into 72 first-order sub-regional units: 21 governorates in Yemen (5.498 cells), 13 provinces in Saudi Arabia (24.614 cells), 11 governorates in Oman (3.895 cells), nine emirate and historical neutral-zone polygons in the United Arab Emirates (904 cells), seven municipalities in Qatar (140 cells), six governorates in Kuwait (238 cells) and five governorates in Bahrain (eight cells). Smooth vector boundaries derived from geoBoundaries polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] preserve coastal islands, Musandam's exclave and desert frontiers without blocky raster staircasing.

Seven benchmark horizons structure the longitudinal series: 1971AD (Gulf independence and post-Dhofar consolidation), 1980AD (peak first oil-boom urbanisation), 1992AD (post-Gulf War realignment and Yemen unification), 2004AD (mid-2000s census synchrony across Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Qatar and Oman), 2015AD (pre-war Yemeni plateau and hydrocarbon peak), 2022AD (Saudi digital register census and post-pandemic recovery) and 2025AD (current demographic projection through 2026AD). Every urban settlement is anchored to official national statistical agencies: Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Statistics (GASTAT, censuses of 1974, 1992, 2004, 2010 and 2022) [@Arabia2022Saudi; @Arabia2023Correction], Yemen's Central Statistical Organization (CSO, 1975, 1986, 1988, 1994 and 2004), Oman's National Centre for Statistics and Information (NCSI, 1993, 2003, 2010 and 2020), the UAE's Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre (FCSA, 1968, 1975, 1980, 1985, 1995, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2023), Qatar's Planning and Statistics Authority (PSA, 1970, 1986, 1997, 2004, 2010, 2015 and 2020), Bahrain's Information & eGovernment Authority (iGA, 1971, 1981, 1991, 2001, 2010, 2020 and 2024) and Kuwait's Central Statistical Bureau (CSB, 1970, 1975, 1980, 1985, 1995, 2005, 2011 and 2021).

To project point-level settlement enumerations and aggregate national counts onto continuous 5-arcminute cells without losing rural oasis populations or smearing metropolitan skyscrapers across empty gravel plains, HANDBOOK disaggregates geoBoundaries administrative polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] via strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic scaling. Within each administrative unit, population is distributed across cells using biophysical suitability covariates, coastal and fluvial proximity weights, explicit two-cell urban mask buffers and metric-isotropic radial distance fields derived from non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging. Across the wider MENA and Arabian domain, the underlying spatial kernel was calibrated on 83.857 weighted domestic records grouped into 3.416 Voronoi catchments across 168.112 valid continental cells, with a median Voronoi catchment radius of 32,51 km and a 90th-percentile radius of 40,25 km. Because Regime 3 enforces modern administrative census totals directly onto every matched ADM1 or ADM2 polygon, the kriging surface governs intra-district allocation rather than overriding recorded headcounts.

Where historical boundaries shifted or new cities arose after 1971AD, settlement time series preserve explicit foundation dates so industrial new towns never cast phantom populations backward. Al-Jubaīl in eastern Saudi Arabia enters the urban ledger at its 1975AD royal industrial charter, while earlier twentieth-century oil and port foundations such as Ad-Dammām (1923AD), Al-Aḥmadī (1946AD), Ḥawallī (1906AD), Al-Jahrā' (1850AD), Al-Wakrah (1828AD) and Al-Muḥarraq (1810AD) carry continuous trajectories across the entire 1971AD to 2025AD interval. Subordinate peri-urban districts lying within 2 km of a primary municipal core are consolidated into their parent metropolis in the source ledger to prevent double-counting.

# Testing and Validation

Source reconciliation across all seven statistical jurisdictions evaluated 5.500 candidate urban and rural localities, retaining 5.250 primary centres and excluding 250 duplicate aliases or subordinate suburbs consolidated into canonical urban cores (Table 1). Coverage spans every constituent state, dominated numerically by Yemen's 2004 CSO locality register alongside enriched GASTAT Saudi, NCSI Omani and Gulf municipal records. All 5.250 retained settlements possess verified WGS84 coordinates, census-anchored population series within the 1971AD–2025AD window and documented statistical agency provenance [@Arabia2022Saudi; @Arabia2023Correction].

```{r tab-agency-provenance, results='asis'}
states_ord <- c("Yemen", "Saudi Arabia", "Oman", "Qatar", "United Arab Emirates", "Kuwait", "Bahrain")
agency_map <- c(
  "Yemen" = "CSO (1975-2004)",
  "Saudi Arabia" = "GASTAT (1974-2022)",
  "Oman" = "NCSI (1993-2020)",
  "Qatar" = "PSA (1970-2020)",
  "United Arab Emirates" = "FCSA (1968-2023)",
  "Kuwait" = "CSB (1957-2021)",
  "Bahrain" = "iGA (1941-2024)"
)
exc_cands <- Filter(function (c) identical(c$status, "excluded"), ledger_json$candidates)
fmt_int <- function (n) formatC(as.integer(n), format = "d", big.mark = ".")

ag_rows <- lapply(states_ord, function (st) {
  sub <- Filter(function (e) identical(as.character(e$country), st), sett_json)
  n_inc <- length(sub)
  n_exc <- sum(vapply(exc_cands, function (c) identical(as.character(c$country), st), logical(1)))
  pks <- vapply(sub, function (e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e$population))), numeric(1))
  lead_e <- sub[[which.max(pks)]]
  data.frame(
    State = st,
    Agency = unname(agency_map[[st]]),
    Included = fmt_int(n_inc),
    Excluded = fmt_int(n_exc),
    LeadCentre = paste0(lead_e$name, " (", viscount_fmt_pop(max(pks)), ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_agencies <- do.call(rbind, ag_rows)
all_pks <- vapply(sett_json, function (e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e$population))), numeric(1))
top_all <- sett_json[[which.max(all_pks)]]
tot_row <- data.frame(
  State = "Total Domain",
  Agency = "Seven national bureaus",
  Included = fmt_int(length(sett_json)),
  Excluded = fmt_int(length(exc_cands)),
  LeadCentre = paste0(top_all$name, " (", viscount_fmt_pop(max(all_pks)), ")"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_agencies <- rbind(df_agencies, tot_row)
rownames(df_agencies) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_agencies,
  "National statistical agency provenance, included urban and rural localities and source-ledger exclusions across the seven Arabian Peninsula states (1971AD-2026AD).",
  c("State", "Statistical Agency", "Included", "Excluded", "Leading Settlement (Peak)")
)
```

Cross-checking the geoBoundaries subadministrative disaggregation [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] against recorded census tables demonstrates high numerical fidelity across 233 matched first- and second-order administrative units (Table 2). In Saudi Arabia and Oman, second-order governorate and *wilayat* boundaries (136 ADM2 units in Saudi Arabia across 1992–2022; 53 ADM2 units in Oman across 1993–2020) resolve dense metropolitan corridors separately from empty desert interior districts such as Al Ahsa's vast southern gravel plain. In Yemen, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain, first-order governorates, emirates and municipalities (44 ADM1 units in total) capture sub-national population shifts across 1980–2024. Across the wider continental audit encompassing 29 historical and 2.629 modern units over 83 benchmark years, 65.864 unit-year conservation checks pass within 0,01% of recorded census totals, with a global maximum relative error of 5,845e-08.

```{r tab-subadmin-coverage, results='asis'}
mod_stats <- summary_cache$chapter_modern_subadmin_stats
name_map <- c(
  SAU = "Saudi Arabia",
  YEM = "Yemen",
  OMN = "Oman",
  ARE = "United Arab Emirates",
  QAT = "Qatar",
  BHR = "Bahrain",
  KWT = "Kuwait"
)
mod_rows <- lapply(names(mod_stats), function (iso) {
  st <- mod_stats[[iso]]
  yrs <- unlist(st$years)
  data.frame(
    State = unname(name_map[[iso]]),
    ISO3 = iso,
    Level = st$level,
    Units = formatC(as.integer(st$matched_units), format = "d", big.mark = "."),
    Span = paste0(min(yrs), "-", max(yrs)),
    Series = as.character(length(yrs)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_mod <- do.call(rbind, mod_rows)
rownames(df_mod) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_mod,
  "Subadministrative geoBoundaries unit coverage and census benchmark spans across all seven Arabian Peninsula jurisdictions.",
  c("Jurisdiction", "ISO3", "Admin Level", "Matched Units", "Census Span", "Waves")
)
```

Table 3 lists the eighteen highest-population administrative units directly enumerated in modern national censuses from 1980AD through 2023AD, illustrating how sharply population concentrated into small metropolitan districts. Riyadh governorate (9.272 km²) grew from 3,83M in 1992 to 8,59M in 2022 under GASTAT enumerations, while Makkah Al Mukarramah (5.624 km²) rose from 4,47M to 7,77M and Jiddah (4.325 km²) stood at 3,75M in 2022 [@Arabia2022Saudi]. In the Emirates, Dubai (4.104 km²) expanded more than thirteenfold from 276,3k in 1980 to 3,66M in 2023, Sharjah (2.103 km²) rose more than elevenfold from 159,3k to 1,81M and Abu Dhabi (58.285 km²) grew from 451,8k to 3,79M [@Emirates2011Employer]. Doha municipality (234 km²) jumped fivefold from 234,8k in 1986 to 1,19M in 2020, Farwaniya in Kuwait (150 km²) climbed from 360,2k in 1995 to 1,11M in 2021 and Wilayat Muscat (431 km²) rose from 549,3k in 1993 to 1,3M in 2020. By contrast, Yemen's leading governorates—Ta'izz (2,39M), Al Hudaydah (2,16M), Ibb (2,13M), Hajjah (1,48M) and Dhamar (1,33M) at the 2004 CSO census—represent broad rural-and-town highland or Red Sea provinces rather than single-city enclaves.

```{r tab-top-adm-units, results='asis'}
top_units <- summary_cache$chapter_modern_top_units
adm_rows <- lapply(top_units, function (u) {
  p <- u$pops
  yrs <- sort(as.integer(names(p)))
  y0 <- as.character(yrs[1])
  y1 <- as.character(yrs[length(yrs)])
  early_str <- if (length(yrs) > 1L) paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(p[[y0]]), " (", y0, ")") else "-"
  late_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(p[[y1]]), " (", y1, ")")
  data.frame(
    ISO3 = u$iso3,
    Unit = u$name,
    Level = u$level,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(u$area_km2, 0L),
    Earliest = early_str,
    Latest = late_str,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_adm <- do.call(rbind, adm_rows)
rownames(df_adm) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_adm,
  "Leading first- and second-order administrative census units across the Arabian Peninsula with polygon area and recorded population growth.",
  c("ISO3", "Administrative Unit", "Level", "Area (km²)", "Earliest Census", "Latest Census")
)
```

Comparison of the urban hierarchy across all 5.250 catalogued settlements further checks against spatial distortion. The rank-size distribution yields a steep Zipf exponent of $\alpha = 1{,}334$ ($R^2 = 0{,}948$), confirming strong primate and secondary-metropolis concentration across the peninsula's oil and port corridors alongside an extensive lower tail of Yemeni highland towns and Gulf oasis centres (Figure 4). Note also a methodological contrast documented in Figure 3: whereas the 2010AD continuous census raster reflects exact subadministrative district counts concentrated along coasts and oases, the 72-subregion baseline tables apportion aggregate national-to-regional totals across 35.297 terrestrial pixels, giving large desert provinces a higher baseline share than their sparse settlements alone hold.

# Results

Total population across the Arabian Peninsula rose from 14,6M in 1971AD to 94,8M in 2025AD, adding 80,2M inhabitants in just over half a century (Figure 2). Expansion proceeded fastest during the first two decades after Gulf independence, averaging 4,86% per year between 1971AD and 1980AD (14,6M to 22,4M) and 4,46% per year between 1980AD and 1992AD (reaching 37,8M) as petrodollar construction recruited millions of workers across Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar and Bahrain while high rural fertility lifted Yemen [@Wagle2024Labor; @Dito2013Arab]. Growth moderated to 3,27% annually from 1992AD to 2004AD (55,6M), 2,93% from 2004AD to 2015AD (76,4M) and 2,17% from 2015AD to 2025AD (94,8M), reflecting falling citizen birth rates in GCC states, intermittent pandemic outflows in 2020 and conflict-induced mortality and emigration in Yemen [@GARENNE2025Urbanizati; @Thomas2025Employabil].


Table 4 summarises the territorial sub-regional allocations by sovereign state across five key horizons from 1971AD to 2025AD. Because these regional sub-masks partition the 35.297 terrestrial pixels smoothly from Saudi Arabia's vast interior basins to Bahrain's compact islands, they capture macro-regional expansion across all 72 administrative polygons while maintaining exact aggregate summation at every horizon.

```{r tab-country-series, results='asis'}
regs <- region_json$regions
c_names <- c(
  saudi = "Saudi Arabia (13)",
  yemen = "Yemen (21)",
  oman = "Oman (11)",
  united = "UAE (9)",
  qatar = "Qatar (7)",
  kuwait = "Kuwait (6)",
  bahrain = "Bahrain (5)"
)
yrs_pick <- c("1971", "1992", "2004", "2015", "2025")
c_rows <- lapply(names(c_names), function (pref) {
  keys_m <- names(regs)[startsWith(tolower(names(regs)), pref)]
  sums <- vapply(yrs_pick, function (y) sum(vapply(regs[keys_m], function (r) as.numeric(r$population[[y]]), numeric(1))), numeric(1))
  data.frame(
    Territory = unname(c_names[[pref]]),
    Y1971 = viscount_fmt_pop(sums[1]),
    Y1992 = viscount_fmt_pop(sums[2]),
    Y2004 = viscount_fmt_pop(sums[3]),
    Y2015 = viscount_fmt_pop(sums[4]),
    Y2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(sums[5]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_cs <- do.call(rbind, c_rows)
hl <- summary_cache$headline_series
tot_cs <- data.frame(
  Territory = "Total Peninsula (72)",
  Y1971 = viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["1971"]]),
  Y1992 = viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["1992"]]),
  Y2004 = viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["2004"]]),
  Y2015 = viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["2015"]]),
  Y2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(hl[["2025"]]),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_cs <- rbind(df_cs, tot_cs)
rownames(df_cs) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_cs,
  "Sub-regional mask population series grouped by state from 1971AD to 2025AD across all 72 first-order territorial divisions.",
  c("State (Sub-Regions)", "1971AD", "1992AD", "2004AD", "2015AD", "2025AD")
)
```

## Saudi Arabia

Saudi Arabia dominates the peninsula's geography and metropolitan hierarchy, encompassing roughly 1,91M km² (68,7% of domain area) and 184 catalogued settlements in the enriched GASTAT sub-mask audit. Between 1971AD and 2025AD, its sub-regional aggregate rose from 6,9M to 44,82M, while GASTAT's administrative censuses recorded national headcounts climbing from 16,95M in 1992 to 22,68M in 2004, 27,14M in 2010 and 32,18M in 2022 [@Arabia2022Saudi; @Arabia2023Correction]. Within that national expansion, population shifted decisively away from small desert villages toward three monumental urban corridors: the central Najdi capital axis around Ar-Riyāḍ, the Hijazi Red Sea gateway uniting Jiddah, Makkah and Al-Madīnah, and the Eastern Province oil-and-petrochemical belt anchoring Ad-Dammām, Al-Khubar, Al-Hufūf and Al-Jubaīl.

Ar-Riyāḍ itself grew nearly eighteenfold in the settlement ledger, from 420k in 1971AD (666,8k at the 1974 first comprehensive census) to 2,78M in 1992AD, 4,09M in 2004AD, 5,19M in 2010AD, a peak of 7,68M in 2017AD and 7,46M in 2025AD—making it by far the largest metropolis anywhere between Cairo and Tehran. Under the 2022 GASTAT census, Riyadh governorate reached 8,59M residents across 9.272 km², reflecting administrative consolidation, royal-court ministries, university expansion and Vision 2030 infrastructure employment [@Hkiri2025Correlatin]. On the Red Sea coast, Jiddah expanded from 380k in 1971AD (561,1k in 1974AD) to a peak of 4,7M in 2021AD and 4M in 2025AD (3,75M in the 2022 governorate census), serving as the Kingdom's primary commercial port and pilgrimage entry point alongside King Abdulaziz University [@Ageeli2019Applicatio]. Inland, Makkah swelled from 310k to 2,57M (with Makkah Al Mukarramah governorate reaching 7,77M in 2022) and Al-Madīnah from 160k to 1,52M (2,39M at the governorate level). Along the Gulf coast, Ad-Dammām grew from 95k to 1,49M, flanked by Al-Khubar (441,4k) and purpose-built Al-Jubaīl, which grew from its 1975AD industrial foundation to 511,6k in 2025AD. Secondary provincial poles—Al-Hufūf (786,4k), Tabūk (640,6k), Buraydah (615,7k), Aṭ-Ṭa'if (607,2k), Khamīs Mushaīṭ (576,7k), Ḥā'il (483,6k), Ḥafar al-Bāṭin (417,2k) and Najrān (411,1k)—completed a continental highway urban grid, while the terraced south-western governorate of Jazan packed 1,4M people into just 1.139 km² by 2022.

## Yemen

Yemen presents the peninsula's sharpest demographic paradox: a territory of 455,6k km² with minimal hydrocarbon wealth yet nearly 32M residents by the mid-2020s (24,29M in the sub-regional territorial allocation, rising from 3,74M in 1971AD) and over 1.630 enumerated localities drawn from the 2004 CSO census register. Unlike the GCC states, where expatriate guest workers account for 35% to 88% of national totals, Yemen's growth was overwhelmingly endogenous, propelled by total fertility rates exceeding 7 births per woman into the late 1980s and remaining near 4 into the 2010s [@GARENNE2025Urbanizati]. Yemen's 1994 and 2004 CSO censuses document intense concentration in the rain-fed central and southern highlands and the Tihama coastal plain: Ta'izz Governorate rose from 1,87M to 2,39M, Al Hudaydah from 1,56M to 2,16M, Ibb from 1,67M to 2,13M, Hajjah from 1,09M to 1,48M and Dhamar from 981,7k to 1,33M, while arid eastern Hadhramaut grew from 755,6k to 1,03M across 157.370 km².

At the urban level, Ṣan'ā' experienced the fastest metropolitan surge in southern Arabia, vaulting twentyfold from 115k in 1971AD to 500,9k in 1990AD, 1,71M in 2004AD, a peak of 2,58M in 2012AD and 2,29M in 2025AD. Two political shocks reshaped Yemeni internal migration after 1990AD. First, the sudden return of roughly 800k expatriate workers expelled from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait during the 1990–1991 Gulf crisis overwhelmed rural terraces and swelled informal settlements around Ṣan'ā', Aden (235k in 1971AD to 1,15M in 2025AD), Ta'izz (626,6k) and Al-Ḥudaydah (550,1k) [@Wagle2024Labor; @Dito2013Arab]. Second, armed conflict after March 2015 fractured maritime grain imports, collapsed municipal public health and displaced millions from front-line districts in Ta'izz, Al-Ḥudaydah and Ṣa'dah into highland cities such as Ibb (285,8k), Dhamār (196,4k) and oil-producing Ma'rib, mirroring conflict-displacement fertility and survival stresses observed in other protracted civil wars [@VERWIMP2007Child].

## Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates

Along the western Gulf littoral, four small sovereign states covering just 100k km² combined rewrote the rules of modern urban demography through hyper-urbanisation and contract labour importation. In the United Arab Emirates (70,7k km²), FCSA enumerations trace an extraordinary climb from 1,04M in 1980 to over 10M by 2023 (5,08M in the 9-subregion pixel mask). Dubayy expanded more than fortyfold in the settlement ledger, from 85k in 1971AD (183,2k in 1975AD) to 669,2k in 1995AD, 1,87M in 2010AD and 3,75M in 2025AD (3,66M in Dubai emirate's 2023 census), transforming from a creek entrepôt into a global aviation, finance and re-export hub [@Emirates2011Employer]. Abū Ẓaby grew from 46k in 1971AD to 1,84M in 2025AD (with the wider Abu Dhabi emirate reaching 3,79M in 2023), while inland oasis Al-'Ayn peaked at 766,9k (2017AD), coastal Sharjah emirate climbed from 159,3k in 1980 to 1,81M in 2023 and adjacent 'Ajmān swelled to 585,6k as an affordable commuter belt.

```{r fig3-density, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_modern_arabian_peninsula_density.png",
  "Continuous 2010AD subadministrative census density surface across the Arabian Peninsula (left) and national mean densities in 2025AD (right).",
  "fig:density",
  list(max_height = "0.42\\textheight")
)
```

Qatar and Kuwait followed parallel trajectories of single-metropolis dominance. In Qatar (11,1k km²), PSA censuses chart Doha municipality's leap from 234,8k in 1986 to 412,7k in 2004, 816,4k in 2010 and 1,19M in 2020 during the North Field liquefied natural gas build-out and 2022 World Cup construction wave. Across Qatar's catalogued settlements, Ad-Dawḥah (peaking at 1,31M in 2012AD; 988,2k in 2025AD) and contiguous Ar-Rayyān (906,4k in 2025AD) together absorb over three-quarters of the peninsula's population, supplemented by satellite towns at Umm Ṣalāl Muḥammad (169,6k), Al-Wukaīr (152,4k) and Al-Wakrah (106,8k). Kuwait (17,5k km²), despite severe population dislocation during the 1990–1991 Iraqi occupation and subsequent departures of Palestinian and stateless *Bidun* residents, recovered rapidly under CSB censuses: Farwaniya governorate alone rose from 360,2k in 1995 to 1,11M in 2021, while the wider Kuwait City conurbation (peaking at 2,99M across metropolitan Al-Kuwayt in 2018AD alongside 61k inside the historic inner core in 2025AD) anchors Ḥawallī (1,02M), Al-Farwānīyah (875k), Al-Jahrā' (503,7k), Al-Finṭās (494k), Al-Manqaf (319,3k) and Mubarāk al-Kabīr (300,3k). Island Bahrain (670 km²), the earliest Gulf oil state, registered the highest sustained spatial density in the peninsula (Figure 3), led by Al-Manāmah (260,6k), Al-Muḥarraq (166,4k), Ar-Rifā' (145k) and Madīnat Ḥamād (96,1k).

## Oman

Oman (313k km²) occupies an intermediate position between the city-states of the upper Gulf and rural highland Yemen. Beginning from an overwhelmingly agrarian and maritime baseline after 1970, Oman expanded steadily across its 75 catalogued NCSI localities (1993–2020), while the 11-governorate mask scales to 15,35M in 2025AD (from 2,36M in 1971AD). Unlike Qatar or Kuwait, Omani urbanisation stretched along two distinct corridors: the fertile Batinah coastal crescent stretching northwest from Muscat toward Ṣuḥār, and the monsoon-watered southern enclave of Dhofar centred on Ṣalālah.

Within the Muscat capital region (reaching 1,42M across metropolitan Muscat in 2019AD), suburban expansion westward onto coastal gravel fans outpaced the cramped historic harbour walled between rocky headlands. Thus As-Sīb rose to 533,6k in 2025AD and adjacent Bawshar to 410,8k, while older Maṭraḥ grew more modestly to 261,6k; together, Wilayat Muscat (431 km²) rose from 549,3k in 1993 to 1,3M in 2020 under NCSI counts. Along the Batinah and interior oasis belt, industrial port Ṣuḥār expanded to 248,5k, accompanied by Al-Buraymī (104,5k), Ṣūr (94,9k) and historic *aflaj* capital Nizwā (73,2k). Far to the south across the desert gap of Al Wusta, Ṣalālah expanded to 333,1k as container-port logistics and summer monsoon tourism linked Dhofar to regional trade [@ALFARHAN2019Migrant].

## Urban Hierarchy and Labour Migration

Across all 5.250 catalogued settlements, the Zipf rank-size slope ($\alpha = 1{,}334$, $R^2 = 0{,}948$) ranks among the steepest in modern demographic history (Figure 4). Fourteen settlements exceed 900k inhabitants at peak—thirteen surpassing one million—led by Ar-Riyāḍ (7,68M peak; 7,46M in 2025AD), Jiddah (4,7M peak; 4M in 2025AD), Dubayy (3,75M), Al-Kuwayt (2,99M metropolitan peak), Ṣan'ā' (2,58M peak; 2,29M in 2025AD), Makkah (2,57M), Abū Ẓaby (1,84M), Al-Madīnah (1,52M), Ad-Dammām (1,49M), Muscat (1,42M), Ad-Dawḥah (1,31M peak), Aden (1,15M), Ḥawallī (1,02M) and Ar-Rayyān (906,4k).

```{r fig4-settlements, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig4_modern_arabian_peninsula_settlements.png",
  "Log-log rank-size distribution across 5.250 catalogued settlements (left) and the twelve largest Arabian Peninsula cities by peak population (right).",
  "fig:settlements",
  list(max_height = "0.42\\textheight")
)
```

This extreme metropolitan concentration rests directly on segmented international labour markets. Across the six GCC states, temporary migrant workers—drawn overwhelmingly from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, the Philippines, Egypt and Jordan—routinely account for half to nearly nine-tenths of private-sector employment in construction, domestic care, nursing, retail and hospitality [@Wagle2024Labor; @AlNawafleh2015Managing; @Hameed2021India; @sheikh2025Navigating]. Bilateral labour corridors and remittance flows bind Gulf cities tightly to sending regions in South Asia and the Levant, while wage differentials between nationals and foreign workers, alongside periodic visa amnesties and return waves during oil downturns or the 2020 pandemic, introduce sharp short-term swings into municipal populations that standard fertility-mortality models cannot capture alone [@ALFARHAN2019Migrant; @Thomas2025Employabil; @Valenta2017Comparativ].

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties govern these estimates and bound sub-regional interpretation. First, Yemen has conducted no full national census since December 2004, leaving post-2015 projections for Ṣan'ā', 'Adan, Ta'izz, Al-Ḥudaydah and rural highland governorates dependent on humanitarian displacement tracking, pre-war fertility trends and satellite-informed urban growth rather than direct door-to-door enumeration [@VERWIMP2007Child].

Second, GCC censuses vary in how they enumerate short-term contract labourers living in employer-provided labour camps on metropolitan fringes. Periodic residency crackdowns—most notably Saudi Arabia's 2013 and 2017 expatriate campaigns and the pandemic departures of 2020—caused rapid swings in Riyadh, Jeddah, Dubai and Doha that multi-year census intervals smooth across intercensal curves [@Wagle2024Labor; @Thomas2025Employabil].

Third, boundary granularity differs markedly across sovereign states. Saudi Arabia (136 ADM2 units) and Oman (53 ADM2 units) resolve individual oasis and coastal districts cleanly, whereas UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Yemen rely on coarser ADM1 governorates or emirates, leaving intra-emirate spatial variation in Abu Dhabi (58.285 km²) and Hadhramaut (157.370 km²) dependent on biophysical covariates and urban buffers [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Finally, as noted in Figure 3, the 72-subregion baseline mask tables apportion broad territorial shares by pixel geometry, so readers comparing sub-national administrative counts should consult the recorded ADM1 and ADM2 census figures in Table 3 alongside the continuous surface in Figure 3.

# Conclusion

Between 1971AD and 2026AD, the Arabian Peninsula transitioned from a sparsely populated landscape of desert oases, modest pearling ports and terraced southern highlands into a hyper-urbanised region approaching 95M inhabitants. Two contrasting demographic engines drove that 6,49-fold expansion: hydrocarbon-funded desalination, state employment and circular *kafala* labour migration across Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman on one side, and sustained endogenous fertility followed by war-driven internal displacement across Yemen on the other. By unifying 5.250 catalogued urban and rural localities with 233 matched ADM1 and ADM2 geoBoundaries census districts from GASTAT, CSO, NCSI, FCSA, PSA, iGA and CSB under mass-conserving pycnophylactic scaling and Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) radial interpolation, HANDBOOK provides a consistent spatial-demographic synthesis of the modern peninsula from post-British independence through 2026AD.

# Appendix

## Leading Sub-Regions in the Territorial Mask

Table 5 reports the eighteen highest-population territorial sub-regions staged in the chapter summary cache across all seven benchmark years from 1971AD to 2025AD. Because these regional sub-masks scale smoothly across the 35.297 five-arcminute cells of the peninsula, geographically expansive provinces in Saudi Arabia, Oman and Yemen occupy the upper ranks.

```{r tab-appendix-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_list <- summary_cache$top_subregions
sub_rows <- lapply(sub_list, function (s) {
  p <- s$population
  data.frame(
    Subregion = s$name,
    Y1971 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1971"]]),
    Y1992 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["1992"]]),
    Y2004 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2004"]]),
    Y2015 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2015"]]),
    Y2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(p[["2025"]]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
rownames(df_sub) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Leading eighteen territorial sub-regions across the Arabian Peninsula from 1971AD to 2025AD.",
  c("Sub-Region", "1971AD", "1992AD", "2004AD", "2015AD", "2025AD")
)
```
